what_it_does: An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) transforms a continuous real-world voltage signal into discrete digital numbers that computers can process. Time-domain ADCs are a clever alternative design: instead of measuring voltage directly, they convert it into a time interval (a delay) and then measure that delay with digital circuits. This is attractive because time intervals are easier to measure precisely. However, there is a subtle problem: when the converter's decision-making logic gets into a 'metastable' state—electrically balanced between 0 and 1—the decision can be unpredictable, and this unpredictability does not follow the neat statistical patterns that error-correction schemes expect. This paper solves the problem by pipelining the decision logic: it gives the comparator extra time to make a clean decision before committing to an answer, using additional flip-flops and logic to detect when uncertainty remains, enabling 10-bit accuracy at 3 billion samples per second.
